what_this_is_en:
Every substance named on every line of the enriched markdown of US20100041557A1, read independently of the compound extraction and asked only that one question: not roles, not quantities, not whether the substance matters. `specific` names one substance a reader could identify (a compound, a named mineral or earth, an ISO common name, a defined polymer); `generic` refers to a substance without naming one, and is counted apart, because in this document the class terms ARE how the patent names most of its formulation ingredients (polar organic solvents, aromatic hydrocarbon solvents, anionic and nonionic surface-active substances, protective colloids, rheology modifiers, antifreeze agents, fillers, binders, buffers). Spans are checked against the ENGLISH rendering of the line, which is what verify.py compares them with: `source.text_en.get(n) or source.lines.get(n)`. This patent is in English, so build_enriched.py writes each printed line and then an identical `> EN:` line; the two are two keys over one English text and both carry the same spans, exactly as a German line and its translation do in EP2045236A1. Where the vision pass could not align a paragraph line for line, text_en gives every line of that paragraph the whole paragraph's English, so those lines carry the paragraph's spans; that is the engine's own rule and not a choice made here. Table rows are lines like any other: TABLE 1 and TABLE 2 name the solvents of examples 2 to 13, TABLE 3, TABLE 4 and TABLE 5 name the solvents of the comparative examples, and each of those rows carries its own solvent as a mention. The three `[IMAGE_EXTRACT]` lines 74, 76 and 78 carry the SMILES of tembotrione and of its two drawn enol tautomers I' and I'' as specific mentions, following EP2045236A1 line 61: the molecule really is on that line, and a SMILES joins by structure rather than by string. The molecular formula printed beside each of those SMILES, C17H16ClF3O6S, is not filed as a separate mention.
TWO PRINTED TRAPS, RECORDED AS PRINTED AND NOT MERGED. (1) The patent glosses `2,2-dimethylpropanol` as `tert. amyl alcohol` on lines 291, 292, 303 and 304. Those are two different compounds, neopentyl alcohol and 2-methylbutan-2-ol, and both names are filed as separate specific mentions on every line that prints them; nothing here decides which one the examples actually used. The same paragraph also prints the hyphenated `2,2-dimethyl-propanol`, filed as its own mention, as is the hyphenated form in claim 23. (2) Claim 16, lines 714 and 726, prints the systematic name malformed, `...(2,2,2-trifluoroethoxymethyebenzoyl]...`, with an unclosed bracket and `methye` for `methyl)`; it is filed exactly as the line reads, with a note. Line 305 prints `cylcoheptane` with l and c transposed, and line 51's abstract prints `2,2,2-trifluoro-ethoxymethyl` with an extra hyphen: both are filed as printed. `H2O` in TABLE 2 rows 12 and 13 is filed as `H2O`, which the vision notes confirm against the page image where the OCR layer had read `HO`.
RULES USED, so that a later reader can tell an omission from a decision. Excluded on purpose: plant genera and species (line 544 is a pure species list and carries no mention), crop and weed names, trade and product names (Exxsol, Solvesso, Borresperse, Morwet, Nekal, Sokalan, Mowiol, Lupasol, Attaclay, Kelzan, Rhodopol, Veegum, Silikon SRE, Rhodorsil, Proxel, Acticide, Kathon MK) and the company names beside them, C.I. colour-index designations (the whole of line 600 except `Rhodamin B`, which is a substance name rather than an index entry), instrument and software names (Bruker-AXS D-5000, Mettler Toledo DSC 25, SHELX-97), space group symbols, wavelengths, 2-theta values, d spacings, unit cell parameters and publication numbers (WO 00/21924). Also excluded: formulation FORMS and dosage words (suspension concentrate, SC, OD, WP, WG, powder, granules, dusting agent), physical state words (oil, amorphous solid, crystals, prisms, needles, agglomerates, precipitate), crystal form labels (form A, form B, form C, modification, polymorph, solvate) and process streams (mother liquor, reaction mixture, spray fluid). Three further decisions, each applied everywhere: (a) a bare `solvent` or `solvents` is filed as generic only on a line that names no solvent and carries no qualified solvent class, since elsewhere it is an anaphor back to names that are on the same line; (b) a generic term whose span is a substring of another generic term filed on the same line is not filed twice, so `organic solvent` is filed and the `solvent` inside it is not, while two chemicals that happen to nest, `hexane` inside `isohexane` on line 214, are both filed because both are printed as separate items; (c) `active substance` and `active substances` are filed as generic only where they stand for substances this document never names (the polymorphism discussion on lines 82 to 85, and `other active substances` in the formulation paragraphs), and not where the same line names tembotrione or its form A or C, which is the role word for the compound named in the same breath. By the same reasoning `herbicides` and `safeners` are filed where they stand for unnamed mixing partners (lines 546, 706, 710) and not where they describe tembotrione's own use (`suitable as herbicides`, line 533; `suitable as desiccants`, line 552). Table COLUMN HEADERS (`Solvent`, `1st Solvent`, `2nd Solvent`) are labels and carry no mention, while the same words in the running text of lines 406, 509 and 378 do, because there they stand for solvents the line does not name.
ONE DEPARTURE FROM EP2045236A1, stated because it goes the other way. Materials named as part of the apparatus ARE filed here: `aluminum` (the closed DSC cup, lines 161, 284 and 354), `graphite` (the monochromator, line 368), `polystyrene` (the container of comparative examples 11 to 20, line 479), `ice-water` (the bath of examples 1 to 15) and the generic `oil` of the oil bath on line 437. The exclusion in the brief covers instrument and software NAMES, and these are substances the page names; filing them costs a reviewer a moment and omitting them would have been a silent judgement that a substance named as hardware is not named. `tylose` on line 602 is filed as specific with a note: it is a trade name for a cellulose ether, but it is printed lower case inside a list of materials and reads as one of them. `Xanthan Gum` on line 585 is filed although the page sets a registered mark on it, because it is the substance's name and not a brand.
TWO ELISIONS THAT HAVE NO LITERAL SPAN, so they are filed under the printed string with a note rather than invented: `m- and p-cymene` on line 305, where m-cymene is named only by that elision and `p-cymene` is the only literal span, and `calcium and magnesium sulfate` on lines 564 and 637, where neither `calcium sulfate` nor `magnesium sulfate` is printed in full. Nothing in this file is a span that is not literally on its line.
WHAT THIS CANNOT SEE, and it is the limit of the whole step: this is one language model, Claude Opus 5 (1M context), reading a document that another language model read for the vision pass and that a third pass extracted compounds from. Where this list and the extraction agree, that agreement is weaker evidence than it looks, and where both missed the same substance nothing in this pipeline can see it. Nothing under runs/US20100041557A1/output/ was opened, listed or grepped while this was written; the read was made against input/US20100041557A1-enriched-numbered.md as rendered by verify.py's own Source, and against input/vision/p*.json for the printed-versus-OCR notes. Blank lines carry no key; every other line carries one, including the ones with nothing on them, because 'a reader looked here and found nothing' and 'nobody looked here' must not be the same colour.
verified_en: Every span in this file is a literal substring of the ENGLISH rendering of the line it is filed under, checked with verify.py's own Source class rather than a reimplementation, so this check and the engine read one definition of what line n says in English: `text = source.text_en.get(n) or source.lines.get(n)`. Source constructed cleanly on this document with no patching (786 lines, 34 blank, 752 keys here); rdkit is not installed in this environment and was stubbed for the import alone, which Source never touches. Spans were not typed from memory. The document was grouped into its 363 distinct English line texts and the read was written against those texts; the nine systematic names, in their six different printed spellings, and the three SMILES were extracted from the line text by regex rather than transcribed, because a systematic name typed by hand is exactly the failure this file exists to detect. All 1604 spans were then re-checked one at a time against text_en at the line number each is filed under, and all 1604 pass. A second sweep looked for every span recorded anywhere in this file appearing on a line where it was NOT recorded, and for chemical-looking tokens on lines given no mention at all; both sweeps were resolved before this file was written, and the first of them is what caught claim 28 (lines 775 and 776) having been missed entirely on the first pass.
